newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine trade gap within estimates-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Philippine trade gap within estimates-analysts.

text.p: A wider Philippine trade gap, announced on Thursday, was within expectations but the liklihood of a further deterioration means the peso needs to depreciate, analysts said.
The deficit in the first two months of the year rose to $1.96 billion from the year earlier's $1.58 billion.
Imports rose 19 percent to $5.5 billion in the two-month period, while exports grew by 16 percent to $3.5 billion.

"It's very well within the government target," said Emma Pante, an economist of Far East Bank. The Philippine Central Bank had earlier projected the trade deficit at $13.8 billion in 1997 from $11.79 billion in 1996.
But analysts said the figure could widen to up to $15 billion this year due to the import of $1.0 billion worth of aircraft.
The growing trade deficit calls for a gradual depreciation of the peso, analysts said.
"I think the peso should go to 27 pesos to allow the economy to absorb the pressures from the trade deficit," said Jose Salceda, research director of SBC Warburg.
It is currently about 26.35 to the dollar.
The Asian Development Bank, in its report released on Thursday, echoed the sentiment.

"Although it is unclear to what extent the appreciation of the peso contributed to this deterioration (in the trade deficit), further appreciation will put pressure on the trade balance, unless productivity in the tradeable goods sector keeps pace."
"The imports are still largely capital equipment," ING Barings research head Jose Cuyegkeng, adding that this would help the economy sustain its growth.
Capital goods increased 23.4 percent in February to $933 million, while consumer goods fell by 18 percent to $213 million.
But, the 16 percent export growth in the first two months was a drop from last year's 32 percent growth due to a contraction in garment exports, analysts said.
